Several goals, one saving budget: deadlines can matter as much as the total

Four graphics compare shared saving capacity, goal deadlines, two allocation rules and the effect of more time or a larger budget.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore three goals sharing one monthly budget

Interactive planning lab

Minimum constant budget for deadline-first funding$1,000
Unfunded by deadlines · deadline first$3,600
Unfunded by deadlines · equal shares$5,400

Hypothetical remaining nominal CAD targets with no opening earmarked balances, interest, inflation or account restrictions. One shared contribution arrives at each month-end, including a deadline month. Deadline-first funding fills the earliest unfinished goal and spills to the next; equal shares divide each month among all active unfinished goals and redistribute capped shares. Tied deadlines use goal letter. A goal freezes after its deadline and receives no later contribution. Funding earmarks money; actual purchases are not modeled. Unused budget is tracked separately, not assigned twice. These mechanical rules do not rank the personal importance of goals.

The central idea

A dollar earmarked for one goal cannot also fund another. Compare each deadline with cumulative saving capacity, and make the allocation rule visible.

01

Write each remaining amount beside its own deadline

The FCAC’s goal-setting guidance starts with priorities, amounts and timeframes. This illustration puts three remaining funding amounts on one calendar so their claims on the same monthly budget can be seen together.

Enter only the money still to be raised for each goal. Existing earmarked savings have already been accounted for before these inputs. Amounts are fixed nominal CAD targets for their payment dates; the model applies no additional inflation or investment return.

The default goals require CAD 6,000 by month twelve, CAD 12,000 by month twenty-four and CAD 18,000 by month thirty-six. Their labels remain A, C and B respectively because each input keeps its own identity when dates change. The shared month-end saving budget is CAD 900.

02

Check cumulative obligations at every deadline

At month twelve, cumulative funding due is CAD 6,000. At month twenty-four it is CAD 18,000, including the earlier goal. At month thirty-six it reaches CAD 36,000. The obligation chart steps up at those dates and compares the totals with the shared budget accumulated over time.

A CAD 900 monthly budget supplies CAD 32,400 over thirty-six months. It cannot fully fund CAD 36,000 under this zero-return model. A positive final saving total is therefore not evidence that all goals fit the plan.

The minimum constant budget for the deadline-first rule is the largest cumulative amount due divided by its deadline month. The default checks are CAD 500, CAD 750 and CAD 1,000 per month. The binding figure is CAD 1,000, assuming saving can begin now and funds can be earmarked early without restrictions.

03

Compare two explicit allocation rules

Deadline-first funding fills the earliest unfinished goal, then sends remaining cash to the next one. Under the default CAD 900 budget, A and C reach their full targets by their own deadlines. B receives CAD 14,400 by month thirty-six, leaving CAD 3,600 unfunded.

The equal-share rule divides each month’s contribution among all active unfinished goals. If a share would exceed a goal’s remaining need, the excess is redistributed within the same month. A goal stops receiving money after its deadline, even when it was not fully funded.

In the default equal-share case, A has CAD 3,600 at month twelve and C has CAD 9,000 at month twenty-four. B eventually reaches CAD 18,000. The shortfalls at A and C’s deadlines total CAD 5,400. Equal monthly amounts are not the same as equal progress toward different deadlines.

04

Later unused cash cannot repair an earlier missed date

The equal-share example leaves CAD 1,800 of the thirty-six-month contribution capacity unallocated after the remaining active goal has been funded. That later money is recorded separately. The model does not move it backward in time to make the missed deadlines appear successful.

The cumulative-funding chart shows the amount earmarked in time under each rule. It is not a cash-account balance after purchases, and the model does not simulate the purchases themselves. Recorded goal funding remains committed once and is not reused for another goal.

Deadline ties are resolved by goal letter in the deadline-first case. Both rules cap funding at a goal’s remaining target. A zero target needs no contributions, and a zero budget leaves every positive target unfunded. These conventions make the comparison reproducible.

05

Test amounts, timing and priorities together

The matrix supplies alternative monthly budgets and scales all selected deadlines, rounding to whole months with a one-month minimum. Goal amounts remain unchanged. Each cell totals shortfalls at the individual deadlines under the deadline-first rule.

The minimum-budget metric is an arithmetic feasibility threshold for this model. It assumes no restricted accounts, no return, no opening funding and divisible month-end contributions. It does not establish affordability in the household budget or decide which goal should have priority.

A real review may change an amount, postpone a flexible date or give a personally important goal precedence over another. The charts expose the consequence of a chosen rule; they do not rank the value of the goals. Record that judgment separately from the calculation so timing and personal priorities remain understandable.
